Title: Graph Neural Networks Based Analog Circuit Link Prediction - ScienceDirect
# Graph Neural Networks Based Analog Circuit Link Prediction. Circuit link prediction, which identifies missing component connections from incomplete netlists, is crucial in analog circuit design automation. However, existing methods face three main challenges: (1) Insufficient use of topological patterns in circuit graphs reduces prediction accuracy; (2) Data scarcity due to the complexity of annotations hinders model generalization; (3) Limited adaptability to various netlist formats restricts model flexibility. We propose Graph Neural Networks Based Analog Circuit Link Prediction (GNN-ACLP), a graph neural networks (GNNs) based method featuring three innovations to tackle these challenges. One main task of analog design automation is circuit link prediction, which infers missing component interconnections from incomplete netlists. proposed the Directional Equivariant Hypergraph Neural Network (DE-HNN) for effective representation learning on directed hypergraphs, particularly for circuit netlists in chip design (Luo et al., 2024). GNNs can leverage the inherent graph structure of circuit netlists, making them well-suited for circuit link prediction. To overcome these obstacles, we propose **GNN-ACLP**, a GNN-based method for analog circuit link prediction, as demonstrated in Fig. 1. **(1)** We formulate circuit link prediction as an undirected graph link prediction problem, where nodes represent circuit components and edges denote connections. We then apply the pipeline to two small-scale datasets and integrate them into a single, unified large-scale dataset, **SpiceNetlist**, to support the training and evaluation of circuit link prediction methods. **GNN-ACLP**, a port-level accurate circuit link prediction method based on the SEAL framework using GNNs. To the best of our knowledge, no previous research has investigated circuit link prediction at the port level, unlike existing component-level methods. **SpiceNetlist**, a novel circuit netlist dataset comprising 775 annotated circuits in both SPICE and JSON formats, featuring 10 component types to facilitate training and evaluation of circuit link prediction methods. Regarding the challenge of the circuit link prediction problem, there are few open datasets available. We propose GNN-ACLP, a novel graph neural networks based framework with SEAL framework integration, achieving port-level accuracy in analog circuit link prediction. Additionally, we create the SpiceNetlist dataset for training and evaluation of circuit link prediction methods. ### Masala-CHAI: A large-scale SPICE netlist dataset for analog circuits by harnessing AI.

results.title: GNN-ACLP: Graph Neural Networks based Analog Circuit Link Prediction
results.content: GNN-ACLP: Graph Neural Networks based Analog Circuit Link Prediction. Circuit link prediction identifying missing component connections from incomplete netlists is crucial in automating analog circuit design. However, existing methods face three main challenges: 1) Insufficient use of topological patterns in circuit graphs reduces prediction accuracy; 2) Data scarcity due to the complexity of annotations hinders model generalization; 3) Limited adaptability to various netlist formats. First, we introduce the SEAL (Subgraphs, Embeddings, and Attributes for Link Prediction) framework and achieve port-level accuracy in circuit link prediction. To address these, the authors propose GNN-ACLP, a novel framework that integrates GNNs with the SEAL (Subgraphs, Embeddings, and Attributes for Link Prediction) methodology for port-level link prediction. Finally, the authors construct SpiceNetlist, a large-scale annotated dataset comprising 775 circuits across 10 component types in both SPICE and JSON formats, to support training and evaluation. The integration of these innovations is illustrated in Figure 1, which provides an overview of the GNN-ACLP framework, showing how input netlists are processed through format conversion, graph construction, and GNN-based prediction. The circuit link prediction problem is formally defined as a graph-based task where nodes represent component ports and edges denote connections. Given a partial netlist missing connections for a specific component, the goal is to predict the correct port-level links. This is framed as Problem 2.2 in the paper, where a node is removed from the graph and its neighbors must be predicted based on the remaining structure and the known component type. The authors adopt the SEAL framework, which generates enclosing subgraphs around potential links and uses Double-Radius Node Labeling (DRNL) to encode structural roles within these subgraphs. **Figure 2: Illustration of the circuit link prediction problem. The core of the proposed solution lies in the adaptation of the SEAL framework for analog circuit link prediction. This labeling scheme effectively distinguishes different structural roles (e.g., common neighbors, bridge nodes) and preserves symmetry, making it highly suitable for link prediction. **Figure 3: Architecture of our circuit link prediction architecture with SEAL.**. In contrast, GNN-ACLP models individual ports as distinct nodes, enabling precise prediction of which specific ports are connected. This methodology enables GNN-ACLP to achieve state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining structural labeling with deep learning on circuit graphs.

results.content: ## Graph Neural Networks Based Analog Circuit Link Prediction. Circuit link prediction, which identifies missing component connections from incomplete netlists, is crucial in analog circuit design automation. However, existing methods face three main challenges: 1) Insufficient use of topological patterns in circuit graphs reduces prediction accuracy; 2) Data scarcity due to the complexity of annotations hinders model generalization; 3) Limited adaptability to various netlist formats restricts model flexibility. We propose Graph Neural Networks Based Analog Circuit Link Prediction (GNN-ACLP), a graph neural networks (GNNs) based method featuring three innovations to tackle these challenges. First, we introduce the SEAL (learning from Subgraphs, Embeddings, and Attributes for Link prediction) framework and achieve port-level accuracy in circuit link prediction. Finally, we build a comprehensive dataset, SpiceNetlist, comprising 775 annotated circuits of 7 different types across 10 component classes. However, its linear computational complexity makes processing large-scale netlists challenging and requires future addressing.
